newsitem.title: ITALY: Cuba's Castro says summit a shameful fig leaf.
newsitem.headline: Cuba's Castro says summit a shameful fig leaf.

text.p: Cuba's communist President Fidel Castro equated hunger with genocide on Saturday and blasted the aims of a World Food Summit to ease starvation as a shameful fig leaf for capitalist domination.

The veteran revolutionary also mounted a fresh attack on the 34-year-old U.S. embargo against his Caribbean island, calling sanctions criminal and absurd in a passionate speech to the U.N.-sponsored summit in Rome.

"Hunger, the inseparable companion of the poor, is the offspring of the unequal distribution of the wealth and the injustices in this world. The rich do not know hunger," Castro told the summit in a speech followed by loud applause.

"If the world is rightly moved by accidents and natural or social catastrophes that bring death to hundreds or thousands of people, why is it not equally moved by that genocide which is taking place every day in front of our eyes?

"Intervention forces are organised to prevent the death of hundreds of thousands of people in eastern Zaire. What are we going to do to prevent the starvation of one million people every month in the rest of the world?" Castro asked.
"It is capitalism, neoliberalism, the laws of a wild market, the external debt, underdevelopment and the unequal terms of reference that are killing so many people in the world."

Castro, dressed in a blue business suit after flying in from Havana early on Saturday in his trademark military fatigues, was given a prominent role at the summit which opened on Wednesday by being appointed one of its six vice-chairmen.

The 70-year-old president, surrounded by tight security, was expected to meet Italian leaders in Rome but it was unclear whether he would have an historic audience with Pope John Paul. The Vatican has said Castro will be received if he asks.

A meeting between the world's most famous communist and the Roman Catholic Pontiff would cement improving relations and could blaze a trail for a papal trip to Cuba, the only Spanish-speaking country in Latin America he has not visited.

The five-day summit at the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), which ends on Sunday, has already adopted a non-binding plan of action to halve the number of people afflicted by chronic hunger and malnutrition by 2015.
"What kind of cosmetic solutions are we going to provide so that in 20 years from now there would be 400 million instead of 800 million starving people?" Castro asked.
"The very modesty of these goals is shameful....Let the truth prevail and not hypocrisy and deceit," he said.

He blasted "the offensive opulence and the squandering by consumer societies", military spending by the rich world and arms sales to developing states. "What are those weapons for if not to dominate the world?" Castro asked.

Castro travelled to Rome buoyed by fresh international condemnation of a U.S. trade embargo imposed in 1962 to try to topple Castro from power. The U.N. General Assembly voted on Tuesday by its biggest majority in five years to lift the ban.

The U.S. Helms-Burton law, which gives Cuban-Americans the right to sue foreign companies that own or operate properties seized by the government after the 1959 revolution, has also been criticised by many of Washington's partners.

"Why is it that criminal policies and absurd blockades that include food and medicine are being added to all this with the purpose of annihilating whole populations out of hunger and diseases?" Castro asked.
"Where is the ethic, the respect for the most basic human rights and the common sense of such policies?"
